strengths: Well-motivated integration of learned components with SR1 quasi-Newton framework, including a principled approach to enforcing secant constraint and positive semi-definiteness through penalty-based regularization

Strong experimental validation on analytic functions with effective progression from controlled quadratics to performance profiles across varying dimensions, clearly demonstrating generalization and the value of the learned projection mechanism
Elegant dimension-invariant architecture using element-wise operations that enables training on low-dimensional problems (N=2) and testing on high-dimensional ones (N=1000) without retraining

Significant practical benefits demonstrated in HMR: achieves competitive accuracy (51.58 PA-MPJPE) with substantially smaller model (10.4M vs 17.4M parameters) while requiring no annotated data or explicit fine-tuning
Comprehensive experimental documentation with detailed hyperparameters, architectural specifications, and ablation studies in appendices, supporting reproducibility
Clear presentation with well-designed figures (particularly Figures 2-3) and thorough related work coverage
weaknesses: Critical gap in comparing to related learned second-order methods (Li et al. [29], Gärtner et al. [17], Ayad et al. [5] are cited but not experimentally evaluated against), making it unclear whether benefits stem from SR1 structure, projection mechanism, or overall design

Secant constraint enforcement is indirect—implemented as soft penalty in meta-loss (Eq. 9) rather than explicit projection during inference. Algorithm 1 does not show constraint verification. No analysis of actual secant constraint violations ||p_k - B_k q_k||_2 during deployment
Misleading framing of 'learned projection'—the method uses a penalty regularization during training, not an explicit projection operator. This obscures the actual mechanism and theoretical guarantees

Modest practical improvements when accounting for iteration costs in HMR: L-SR1 requires 13 iterations to reach 51.58 PA-MPJPE while LGD reaches 55.90 in 4 iterations; at equal 4-step comparison, improvements exist but are less dramatic than claimed
Limited scope of real-world validation to single application (HMR). Unclear whether benefits generalize to other optimization-based tasks, neural network training, or different problem structures
Hyperparameter λ_sec varies dramatically (100 for quadratics, 10 for profiles, 1 for HMR) without principled guidance or sensitivity analysis, raising reproducibility and generalization concerns

Missing ablation studies: no comparison of learned vs. fixed learning rates, learned vs. classical SR1 vector generation, or impact of buffer size L. No analysis of necessity of learned projection mechanism

strengths: Addresses an underexplored direction (learned second-order optimization) with principled grounding in quasi-Newton methods
Dimension-invariant design enables generalization across problem sizes without retraining
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning quadratic functions, benchmark functions, and real-world HMR task
Honest discussion of limitations (computational overhead) in appendix
Achieves competitive HMR results with smaller model size than learned first-order baseline (10.4M vs 17.4M parameters)
weaknesses: 'Learned projection' mechanism is fundamentally misrepresented: it is merely a soft penalty term (λ_sec · ||p_k - B̃_k q_k||²₂) added to training loss, not a true projection; PSD guarantee via B₀ + Σv_i v_i^T is trivial and non-novel; critically, the secant constraint is only softly enforced during training with no guarantee of satisfaction at test time, creating a gap between formulated problem (Eqs. 6-8) and implementation

Limited technical novelty: core contribution reduces to standard MLPs generating vectors and learning rates integrated into SR1, which is incremental relative to prior learned second-order methods (Li et al. [29], Gärtner et al. [17])

Weak experimental validation: L-BFGS substantially outperforms L-SR1 on quadratics (Fig. 3a); performance profiles show only marginal advantages over Adam/LBFGS; in HMR, comparison is primarily against a first-order learned method (LGD) with no evaluation against classical second-order solvers (LBFGS, L-BFGS), and 7.4% improvement is modest
Missing critical comparisons: paper cites Li et al. [29] and Gärtner et al. [17] as related learned second-order optimizers but does not compare against them—a fundamental oversight

Generalization claims are insufficiently supported: quadratic experiments train on N=2 and test on N=10 (5× jump); performance profiles show inconsistent generalization across very different dimensions (50-1000); single real-world domain without cross-domain evaluation

Misleading 'self-supervised' framing: meta-training on optimization examples is a form of supervision; HMR involves AMASS dataset with annotated 3D poses; terminology obscures actual data requirements

No convergence analysis or theoretical justification: no proof that minimizing Eq. 9 ensures good test-time optimization behavior; gap between soft training-time constraint and test-time secant satisfaction is unexplained

Incomplete computational analysis: per-iteration cost is higher than Adam; L-SR1 requires 13 iterations vs LGD's 4 for HMR; total wall-clock time comparison missing, so claimed efficiency gains are unquantified

Insufficient ablation studies: Table 3 only varies hidden dimension and encoder inputs; no ablations on component contributions (e.g., vector generator vs. learning rate generator), secant loss sensitivity, or buffer size effects

HMR evaluation incomplete: single dataset (3DPW); no classical second-order baseline (LBFGS); confounding factors (architectural differences, hyperparameter tuning, additional self-supervised loss term in Eq. 13) not isolated; unknown how much improvement is optimizer-driven

strengths: Novel approach to learned second-order optimization: Addresses underexplored area by combining SR1 Quasi-Newton methods with learned neural modules, filling a gap where most learned optimizers focus on first-order methods
Principled theoretical framework: Well-grounded in optimization theory with motivated design for maintaining secant constraints and positive semi-definiteness properties of Quasi-Newton methods
Strong empirical results on HMR: 3.7% improvement over LGD baseline (51.58 vs 55.90 PA-MPJPE) with 39% smaller model and 18% faster inference, demonstrating practical utility
Dimension-invariant architecture: Element-wise operations enable generalization across problem dimensions without retraining, a valuable practical property

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Well-designed experiments spanning controlled analytics (quadratics, benchmarks), real-world application (HMR), ablations, and performance profiles with clear methodology
Self-supervised training without fine-tuning: Demonstrates data efficiency compared to existing learned optimization baselines
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed implementation details, comprehensive appendix with hyperparameters, architectures, and additional experiments
weaknesses: Unclear enforcement of key constraints: The learned projection mechanism claims to ensure both PSD and secant condition satisfaction, but PSD-ness follows from outer product structure while secant compliance relies only on training penalty term—no empirical validation that secant condition is satisfied at test time

Limited theoretical analysis: No convergence guarantees, rates, or characterization of when learning improves over classical SR1; lacks explanation for why learned method outperforms LBFGS on quadratics (theoretically optimal for this class)

Narrow experimental scope for generalization claims: Quadratic experiments use modest 5× scaling (N=2→10); HMR operates in 82-dimensional space, far smaller than typical deep learning; no large-scale neural network training experiments where learned optimizers have greatest impact

Limited baseline comparisons: HMR evaluation compares only to LGD [54]; missing comparisons to recent HMR methods (WHAM, PromptHMR), classical LBFGS on same task, and other learned second-order methods from related work

Meta-training specificity: Performance profiles experiment uses meta-training on exact problem classes being evaluated (quadratics, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin), raising generalization concerns; only HMR demonstrates transfer to different problem structure

Incremental component novelty: Individual components (standard MLPs, outer products for preconditioning, penalty-based constraints) lack architectural or algorithmic innovation; contributions are largely in combination rather than individual elements

Runtime overhead not fully addressed: Acknowledged higher runtime vs first-order methods; justification (gradient computation bottleneck) may not apply broadly; total wall-clock time for HMR not reported

Insufficient hyperparameter analysis: Multiple critical hyperparameters (buffer size L, learning rate generators γ₁/γ₂, secant weight λ_sec) with limited sensitivity study; Table 3 ablations only cover hidden dimension and encoder inputs

Presentation clarity issues: Input feature selection (x_k-1, p_k-1, d_k-1, g_k-1, q_k-1) not well justified; distinction between learned vs. classical SR1 components could be clearer; implementation of projection optimization (Eq. 6-8) not detailed
Missing interpretability and analysis: No investigation of learned vector properties, failure modes, or sensitivity to problem structure; limited insight into what the neural modules actually learn

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing underexplored learned second-order optimization
Principled technical design of PGSM with PSD-by-construction rank-one parameterization and secant-guided meta-training
Dimension invariance through element-wise operations enables transfer across problem sizes without retraining
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with controlled quadratics, performance profiles, and real-world HMR application
Practical improvements on HMR with smaller models (10.4M vs 17.4M parameters) and no task-specific fine-tuning
Extensive implementation details and ablations support reproducibility
Honest limitations discussion in appendices
weaknesses: Lacks descent direction guarantees due to coordinate-wise learning rates applied to PSD preconditioner; justified only by empirical behavior during meta-training
Limited real-world validation: only HMR tested despite claims about broad applicability to optimization-based pipelines
Modest empirical improvements on HMR (51.74 vs 55.90 mm PA-MPJPE, ~4.2% over LGD); PGSM contributes only ~2% additional gain over variant without secant penalty
Incomplete analysis of when secant constraint is beneficial versus restrictive for non-convex problems
Limited algorithmic novelty: combines standard MLP architectures (following Gärtner et al. 2023, Metz et al. 2022) with straightforward secant penalty; no new theoretical principles
Computational cost incompletely addressed: while faster per-iteration than LGD (91 ms vs 166 ms), modest accuracy gains and task-dependent trade-offs not thoroughly analyzed
Generalization across dimensions conflates optimization difficulty with true generalization (AUC increases at higher dimensions under fixed iteration budget)
Missing comparisons with other recent learned second-order optimizers (Liao et al. 2023, Gärtner et al. 2023)
Multiple hyperparameters (L, K, λsec, γ₁, γ₂) introduced with limited sensitivity analysis; unclear how to set these for new domains
Performance profile experiments show relatively small margins versus baselines, suggesting task-specific tuning rather than fundamental superiority
